statement: Eight parcels all have different weights. A balance compares two parcels at a time, one on each pan, and shows which one is heavier. What is the smallest number of weighings that is certain to find the heaviest parcel, however the results turn out?

choices.misconception: I counted the rounds of a knockout, 8 to 4 to 2 to 1, instead of the weighings, but each round needs several weighings.
I counted only the first round, pairing the 8 parcels into 4 weighings, and forgot that the winners must be compared too.
I thought every parcel had to be weighed once, so I counted one weighing per parcel.
I compared every pair of parcels, $8 \times 7 \div 2 = 28$ weighings, which is far more than needed.

hints: After a weighing, which parcel can no longer be the heaviest?
Each weighing can rule out at most one parcel, the lighter one, from being the heaviest. Count how many parcels must be ruled out, and check that a knockout really manages it in that many weighings.
Seven parcels must be ruled out, and each weighing rules out only one.

solutions.reliable: A knockout works: weigh any two parcels, keep the heavier, weigh it against a new parcel, and so on. Each weighing knocks out one parcel, so after 7 weighings only one is left, and it has beaten every other parcel directly or through a chain. Fewer weighings are not enough: a weighing only shows that one parcel is lighter than another, so it rules out at most one parcel. To be sure which parcel is heaviest, all 7 others must have lost at least once, which needs at least 7 weighings. The answer is 7. The transferable idea: when each test can eliminate at most one candidate, you need at least as many tests as candidates to eliminate.

whyOnTest: Tests balance reasoning: each weighing can only eliminate one candidate, so a knockout is best, and rounds are not the same as weighings.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
